title: The sower again (Mark 4:1–20)
hook: now read the parable with the explanation beside it
tomorrow: the seed that grows while you sleep

segments.voice: Yesterday, a family widened to everyone who does God's will. Your line was family by doing God's will. Today, a farmer you've met before.

A farmer flinging seed: some on the path, some on rock, some in thorns, some on good soil. You've met him before, back in the stories camp, in Matthew's gospel. That time, it was a story. Now, reading Mark straight through, he comes back in Mark's own words, and this time you can do what a good reader does: lay the story beside the explanation Jesus gives his friends afterward, and look closely at one kind of ground.
screen: `A FARMER FLINGING SEED.` → `NOW IN MARK'S WORDS.` → `STORY AND EXPLANATION, SIDE BY SIDE.`

segments.voice: First, the setting. The crowd is so big that Jesus gets into a boat and sits on the water, teaching the people on the shore. He begins, in the Douay-Rheims: "Hear ye: Behold, the sower went out to sow." Four kinds of ground. Seed on the path is eaten by birds. Seed on rock springs up fast and withers in the sun, with no root. Seed among thorns is choked. Seed on good ground yields thirty, sixty, a hundredfold. And he ends: he that hath ears to hear, let him hear. Second, the explanation. Later, alone with the twelve, Jesus explains it line by line. The seed is the word. The path is the person the word never gets into. The rock is the one who welcomes it with joy but falls away when trouble comes. Good ground is the one who hears, receives, and bears fruit. Third, the thorns, and there's nothing dramatic about them. "And the cares of the world, and the deceitfulness of riches, and the lusts after other things entering in choke the word, and it is made fruitless." The thorns don't kill the seed on the first day. It sprouts. It grows. It's just slowly crowded out by worry, by money, by wanting other things, until nothing comes of it. Nobody decides to stop listening. It gets choked. Fourth, the harvest. Thirty, sixty, a hundredfold: some readers hear that last number as astonishing to people who farmed. The parable ends not in failure but in abundance.
screen: `A BOAT FOR A PULPIT.` · `PATH, ROCK, THORNS, GOOD GROUND.` · `THE THORNS: WORRY, MONEY, WANTING.` · `THIRTY, SIXTY, A HUNDREDFOLD.` · then, large: `THE CARES OF THE WORLD CHOKE THE WORD.`

segments.voice: Look back over the last few days: what choked the good things? Not a disaster, just the slow crowding, a worry you kept circling, money on your mind, wanting something so much it filled the room. Name one thorn and see it clearly, without pulling it out yet; if you pray, show it to God, and if you don't, notice how much room it takes up.
The sower again. The parable of four kinds of ground, read now in Mark, with Jesus's own explanation beside it. Today's word.
Your line: the thorns are the cares. Good ground still gives a hundredfold. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Catholics hear the parable of the sower at Sunday Mass in Ordinary Time, and some use it for lectio divina, asking which kind of ground they are right now.

original.note: Greek: thorns, the thistles and briars that choke the growing seed.

trapdoor: what you thought: a farming story about seeds.
what it means: the same word lands differently; the thorns are the everyday cares that slowly choke it.
what a scholar hears: a parable with its own explanation attached, each ground read as a kind of hearer, ending in thirty, sixty, a hundredfold.

notes: Douay-Rheims Mark 4:3 and 4:19 given from memory; confirm.
The hook refers back to the Matthew version of the sower in camp 2 (the outline's 'The sower (Matthew 13:1–23)'); confirm the day is taught before this one on the Catholic path.
Hundredfold as 'astonishing': ancient yield estimates vary (often cited as around tenfold for good years); stated loosely.
Mark 4:10–12 (the purpose of parables, quoting Isaiah) is not discussed.
